activities.anchor: The modal status of a claim is a metaphysical question
activities.caption: file each claim by modal status
activities.name: modalStatusSort

config.prompt: Worlds, not confidence — file each claim by its modal status:
buckets: necessary — true in all possible worlds

items.label: "water is H₂O" — discovered by chemistry, yet fixed across every world with water
the Eiffel Tower standing in Paris

config.why: Modal status is a fact about how a claim sits across possible worlds, not about how confident anyone is in it — the two "could it have been otherwise?" questions look grammatically identical but differ totally in answer.

activities.anchor: Both swap a modal notion for an epistemic one
activities.caption: find the faulty line — confidence is not modality
activities.name: modalEpistemicSpot

config.prompt: One line of this student's gloss on modal status is wrong — click it:
lines: "Necessary" means very well established; "possible" means not yet ruled out.
Everyday speech uses "must" and "might" for confidence, not for worlds.
"There are nine planets" was once as certain as arithmetic — and still necessary.
"Water is H₂O" was a chemical discovery, yet once true it is necessary.
Modal status is about how a claim sits across possible worlds, not about confidence.
config.correction: It was once as certain as arithmetic — and turned out contingent through and through. Certainty is no guide to modal status; only worlds decide it.
config.why: Both swaps trade a claim about worlds for one about our evidence — the classic beginner error this section dismantles.

activities.caption: pair each axiom with its frame condition
activities.name: modalAxiomMatch

config.prompt: Each axiom of modal logic is equivalent to a condition on accessibility — pair them:

pairs.right: reflexive frames — each world counts as accessible from itself
obligation implies permission — instead of T

config.why: The correspondence between axioms and frame conditions made modal logic a working science: S4 is T + 4, and S5 — necessity absolute across all worlds — is T + 4 + 5.

activities.anchor: points in a formal space of alternatives
activities.caption: drag the divider — two readings of possible worlds
activities.name: modalWorldsCompare

config.prompt: Drag the divider between the two readings of possible worlds:

before.label: Tools, not planets
before.text: Abstract representations of complete ways things could have been — devices for tracking consequence. Nobody must believe other worlds exist; the semantics is an exact instrument.

after.label: Lewis's modal realism
after.text: David Lewis's audacious claim: the worlds really exist — concrete, spatiotemporally isolated from ours. Whether they exist or are mere devices is a separate metaphysical dispute; the logic runs identically either way.

config.why: Not distant planets or parallel universes a physicist might discover — actualism versus modal realism is a dispute the logic itself never settles.

activities.anchor: The logic is valid — the entire question collapses onto premise (1)
activities.caption: walk the wager — is a maximally great being possible?
activities.name: modalOntoBranch

config.root: The modern ontological argument is valid. Everything collapses onto one premise — walk the wager.

start.text: Premise (1): possibly, a maximally great being exists. Your call?

choices.label: Deny it — maximality is incoherent, like a square circle

theist.text: Then (2) maximal greatness, if instantiated in any world, is instantiated in every world — these properties do not depend on luck — so (3) the being exists in the actual world.

atheist.text: The atheist denies the possibility — not that the argument is invalid, nor even that theism is contradictory, but that maximality itself cannot be instantiated. The wager is now explicit: the argument is exactly as strong as premise (1).

config.why: Modal logic transformed a squabble about "conceiving" into a single, clearly stated wager — atheists deny the possibility, theists affirm it, and everyone can see it.

activities.caption: rebuild the Kalām argument — and its counter
activities.name: modalKalamOrder

config.prompt: Rebuild the Kalām argument, then the objection it must face:
items: Whatever begins to exist has a cause
So the universe has a cause
Hume and Russell press back: why not the universe as a whole necessary?
config.why: If sound, the cosmological family establishes a necessary being — and then all the work moves to identifying it with the personal God of theism. Aquinas conceded the argument gives no acquaintance with God's nature.

activities.caption: file each move in the design-and-evil dialectic
activities.name: modalEvilSort

config.prompt: File each move in the design-and-evil dialectic:

items.label: Paley's watch — intricate spatial order implies a designer
Swinburne's Bayesian case from temporal order — the laws themselves
Mackie's inconsistent triad — God and evil cannot coexist
Rowe's fawn burning slowly in a forest fire no one ever sees
Plantinga's free will defence — transworld depravity keeps the world possible
Hick's soul-making theodicy — evil as the price of the vale

config.why: Since consistency suffices to defeat the logical problem, most philosophers concede that round to the theist and fight on evidential ground — where Hick's soul-making reply carries a probabilistic burden.

activities.anchor: A defence needs only logical consistency
activities.caption: true or false — what a defence must prove
activities.name: modalDefenceJudge

statements.s: Plantinga's free will defence proves that free will explains evil.
statements.why: It claims neither that nor that God remains probable despite evil — a defence needs only possibility.

statements.s: Logical consistency alone defeats the logical problem of evil.
statements.why: If a world with significantly free creatures, some of whom choose wrongly in some circumstances, is possible, the inconsistent triad fails.

statements.s: The defence also answers Rowe's evidential problem — the fawn, the quantity of suffering.
statements.why: The evidential problem is untouched by it; there Hick's soul-making theodicy carries a different, probabilistic burden.

statements.s: Most philosophers now concede the logical round to the theist.
statements.why: Consistency suffices against the logical problem — so the fight moves to evidential ground.
